sentence: **Nov 9, 2026:** VoltaGrid filed an emergency appeal of the Nov 4 order.
**Nov 12, 2026:** The PSC's Chairman issued an order that put the Nov 4 order on hold for now.
**Nov 13, 2026:** The petitioners answered the appeal, and a PSC staff witness filed rebuttal testimony.
The petition asks the Public Service Commission (PSC) to say whether the plan by VoltaGrid, the plant's builder, breaks two power laws.
The petition also asks the PSC to order VoltaGrid to stop any work that breaks those laws.
The first law is the Territorial Act, the Georgia law that assigns service areas to utilities.
The second law is the Cogeneration Act, a 2001 Georgia law on plants that power their owners.
The petition says the Cogeneration Act bars the sale of a plant's power to anyone but an electric supplier.
The hearing will take up four questions.
The first is whether the PSC has power over VoltaGrid as an "electric supplier."
The second is whether the people who filed are "interested parties" who may bring the case.
The third is whether the plan to build the plant, run it and send its energy to the data center breaks either law.
The fourth is whether any PSC action is needed.
The PSC also gave the Hearing Officer, the person the PSC appointed to hear the case, a question of its own.
That question is whether VoltaGrid's service falls under the PSC's power.
If the answer is yes, the Hearing Officer is to ask "what if any action the Commission should take."
After the hearing, the Hearing Officer sends the PSC a recommended decision.
The PSC can adopt that decision.
A state air-permit review describes the plant.
The plant would make up to 90 MW from 33 natural gas engines and run all year.
One megawatt (MW) is a unit of power equal to a million watts.

sentence: Two laws are at issue.
One is the Territorial Act, the Georgia law that assigns service areas to utilities.
The other is the Cogeneration Act, a 2001 Georgia law on plants that power their owners.
This page does not pick an outcome.

**If you care most about neighbors' air, noise and light:** The petition says VoltaGrid, the plant's builder, adds "air, light, and noise pollution to an area already overburdened by these industrial impacts."
**If you care most about freedom to make private on-site power deals:** VoltaGrid says it "has no special privileges, no condemnation power, is the antithesis of a monopoly."

**If you care most about who pays for stranded power lines:** Georgia EMC, a trade group for electric membership corporations (EMCs), says the costs would be "absorbed by the electric supplier’s other consumers."

**If you care most about one set of rules for every power provider:** Georgia Power says a one-customer exception would let any company "render any amount of service, and avoid Commission jurisdiction."
**If you care most about deciding on a full record:** The PSC's staff says an early dismissal "will not serve the Commission’s objective of timely and efficiently resolving the issue."
Three sides share one view: the people who filed, Georgia EMC and Georgia Power each say the PSC has power over VoltaGrid's plan.
**What it does:** The PSC would end the case with no ruling against VoltaGrid's plan.

sentence: Every card uses the same fields in the same order, and all filings cited here are in one docket, or case file, at the Public Service Commission (PSC).

"Supported" means the record we read backs the card's main factual premise and no party we read disputes that premise; "Mixed" means parties give conflicting accounts of the facts; "Uncertain" means the deciding facts are blacked out, missing or not yet known.
"Legal question" marks a card that turns on how a law reads, which the PSC decides; this page does not grade legal questions.
"Claim type" says whether a card rests on facts, law, predictions or a mix.
"Documented" means a party made the argument in a filing, given with its date, and "Side" names the party and the outcome the card supports.
We read the long filings in excerpts found by keyword search, so a card may miss points made elsewhere in a filing.
Cards follow the order in which each side first filed its argument, with VoltaGrid's two arguments together; the order is not a ranking.

**In short:** The petitioners say VoltaGrid, the plant's builder, would sell power to Serverfarm, the data center's owner, in Georgia Power's area, breaking the Territorial Act, the Georgia law that assigns service areas to utilities.
Evidence: Mixed.
**Who says it:** The petitioners, a Newton County nonprofit and four nearby residents, made the argument through their lawyers in the petition filed with the PSC on Jul 13, 2026.

sentence: The petition says: "The Territorial Act prohibits VoltaGrid from furnishing retail electric service to Serverfarm."
The petition also says the plan breaks the Cogeneration Act, a 2001 Georgia law on plants that power their owners, because VoltaGrid "is selling its energy to Serverfarm."
**What supports it:** The petition quotes Serverfarm's air permit papers: "Serverfarm and VoltaGrid are separate companies with no cross ownership or direct control over each other’s operations."
A witness for the PSC's staff said on Nov 13, 2026, that "VoltaGrid is providing an ongoing power-generation and power-delivery service to Serverfarm."
**Who disagrees:** A VoltaGrid executive said in a sworn statement filed with VoltaGrid's Sep 16, 2026, request to dismiss: "VoltaGrid will not sell that electricity to Serverfarm or to anyone else."
**What challenges it:** VoltaGrid said on Oct 26, 2026, that every ban in the Territorial Act applies only to electric suppliers, and VoltaGrid says it is not one.
**What's missing:** The fee amounts in the contract are blacked out in the public copy we read.
The PSC staff's witness said: "I am not a lawyer and do not have an opinion" on the legal classification.
**What's uncertain:** Whether turning a customer's gas into power for a fee is a retail sale is a legal question the PSC has not decided as of Nov 14, 2026.
marker: {editorial: process note; the Nov 4 order says the electric-supplier question is undecided (P-025)}

sentence: **In short:** VoltaGrid says it will serve one customer on that customer's site, not the public, so the PSC has no authority over VoltaGrid.
Evidence: Mixed.
**Who says it:** VoltaGrid made the argument in the brief it filed with the PSC on Sep 16, 2026.
The brief says VoltaGrid does not "furnish service to the public."
A VoltaGrid executive gave the same answer in testimony dated Oct 9, 2026.
**What supports it:** The executive's sworn statement says Serverfarm supplies the gas and "VoltaGrid will not take ownership of the electricity."
The statement says VoltaGrid is not "pursuing any additional customer or business in Georgia."
VoltaGrid's brief says VoltaGrid "has no special privileges, no condemnation power, is the antithesis of a monopoly."

**Who disagrees:** Georgia EMC, a trade group for electric membership corporations (EMCs), said on Oct 16, 2026, that "VoltaGrid conflates" the PSC's power to regulate utilities with its power to enforce the Territorial Act.
Georgia Power said the same day that VoltaGrid's service "is a public service that should be regulated by the Commission."
The petitioners said that, under one reading of the Territorial Act, VoltaGrid breaks the law "regardless of whether VoltaGrid qualifies as an electric supplier."
**What challenges it:** The petitioners said on Oct 16, 2026, that VoltaGrid "has explored serving other Georgia customers."
The PSC staff's witness said the contract's statement of work calls for "phased Power Delivery reaching 90 MW" and states monthly fees per kWh.
MW stands for megawatts, a measure of power, and kWh for kilowatt-hours, a measure of energy.
marker: {analysis: plain-language definitions, not from the cited sources}
